title: The Evidential Problem of Evil
rootClaim: The existence of gratuitous and unnecessary suffering makes the existence of an omnipotent, omniscient, and all-loving God highly improbable.

branches.text: Rowe's Evidential Premise: Instances of intense suffering exist which an omnipotent, omniscient entity could have prevented without losing a greater good or permitting an equal or worse evil.

children.text: Natural Animal Suffering: Billions of years of animal agony (e.g. a fawn trapped in a forest fire) occurred before human existence, serving no moral test or free-will development for humanity.

Skeptical Theism (CORNEA Principle): Humans lack the cognitive capacity to survey all possible cosmic goods and evils; thus, our inability to see a reason for suffering does not prove no reason exists.

Moral Paralysis Counter-Rebuttal: If Skeptical Theism is true, humans can never be morally justified in preventing suffering, as any apparent horrific evil might secretly be necessary for an unknown divine greater good.
Radical Epistemic Skepticism: Skeptical Theism undermines confidence in human moral intuitions and divine revelation, making moral duty and theological knowledge impossible.
Gratuitous Evil Paradox: If even a single instance of truly uncompensated suffering exists, an all-loving and all-powerful God would be morally obligated to prevent it.

branches.text: Arbitrary and Unequal Suffering: Suffering is distributed unevenly and indiscriminately across innocent infants and creatures, rather than proportionally tuned for individual moral growth.

children.text: Logical Inconsistency with Omnibenevolence: An omnipotent and omniscient entity could accomplish any valid pedagogical goal or soul-building objective without inflicting catastrophic trauma.

Soul-Making Theodicy (Hickian View): The world is intentionally designed not as a paradise, but as a challenging environment ('vale of soul-making') where virtue and character must be earned through struggle.
Ruinous Trauma Failure: Extreme suffering frequently destroys human agency, causes permanent psychological ruin, or kills innocent infants before any moral development can take place.

branches.text: Plantinga's Free Will Defense: Moral evil is the result of human free choice, and a world with free creatures capable of moral good necessarily entails the risk of moral evil.

children.text: Inapplicability to Natural Evils: Free will only accounts for human moral actions; it completely fails to explain non-human natural disasters like earthquakes, tsunamis, and disease.
Demonic Agency Hypothesis: Natural evils could theoretically be caused by the free choices of non-human angelic or demonic agents.
Ad Hoc Violation of Ockham's Razor: Positing invisible demons to explain physical laws and natural plate tectonics is an unevidenced, ad hoc hypothesis that degrades explanatory parsimony.

branches.text: Greater Good Theodicy: God permits evil strictly when it is a logically necessary condition for securing a far greater good or preventing a greater evil.

children.text: Limits of Omnipotence: Even an omnipotent being cannot perform logical impossibilities, such as bestowing moral courage without the existence of danger or risk.
Sub-Optimal Universe Design: An all-powerful designer could have established physical laws and neurological pain thresholds that allow moral lessons without horrific gratuitous agony.

definitions.description: The argument advanced by William L. Rowe that while God's existence is logically possible, the presence of gratuitous suffering renders the existence of an omnipotent, omniscient, all-loving God highly improbable.
Suffering that serves no higher moral purpose, yields no outweighing greater good, and prevents no equal or worse evil.
The view that human cognitive limitations prevent us from discerning divine reasons for permitting evil, so our failure to see a reason is not evidence that none exists.
John Hick's philosophical argument that God created the world as an imperfect environment designed for moral development and character growth rather than hedonistic comfort.
Condition of Reasonable Epistemic Access, which states that one is only justified in claiming X does not exist if one could reasonably expect to observe X if it did exist.
